title: Revision and editing
note: Revise from large to small. Higher-order concerns (thesis, audience and purpose, organization, development) come first; lower-order concerns (sentence structure, punctuation, word choice, spelling) come after. Let a draft rest, read it aloud, and reread it as if someone else wrote it.

read.title: Revising from the top down
text: Many writers think revision means fixing commas. Commas matter, but they come last. Revision is literally re-seeing: looking at a draft again and asking whether it does what it should.

Start with the higher-order concerns. Can you state the thesis in one sentence? Does every section serve it? Is the order logical for this audience? Does each paragraph have enough evidence and explanation? A useful tool here is the reverse outline: after drafting, write one line summarizing each paragraph. Gaps, repetitions and detours show up at once.

Only then move to lower-order concerns: sentence structure, word choice, punctuation and spelling. Fixing these first wastes effort, because a paragraph you polish today may be cut tomorrow. The exception is an error so severe that it stops a reader from understanding; that has to be fixed early.

Distance helps at every stage. Set the draft aside for a day if you can. Read it aloud, since the ear catches clumsy rhythm and missing words that the eye skips. And read it as if a stranger wrote it, so you judge the words on the page rather than the ideas in your head.
